Why is Canberra Australia’s capital?

Sydney and Melbourne were rivals for the role. The solution was a new capital, with a location written into the Constitution.

By Biel Sardà · Published 28 Sept 2026 · Suggest a correction

A compromise between two rivals

Sydney may be Australia’s most familiar city, but Canberra is its capital. The choice grew out of a rivalry between New South Wales and Victoria when the colonies federated in 1901.

Rather than give the role to Sydney or Melbourne, the new nation would have a separate seat of government.

At least 100 miles from Sydney

The Constitution required the capital to be in territory within New South Wales, at least 100 miles from Sydney, or about 160 kilometres. Until the new seat of government was ready, Parliament would meet in Melbourne.

That distance rule is quite specific. It did not require the capital to sit halfway between the two cities, even though Canberra is often described as a compromise between them.

A city takes shape

The site of present-day Canberra was selected in 1908. The city was officially named on 12 March 1913, and the federal Parliament moved there in 1927.

Those dates mark different steps: choosing the location, naming the city and making it the working home of Parliament.

Which city came before Canberra?

Where did the federal Parliament meet before moving to Canberra?

Melbourne. It hosted Parliament while the new capital was being established.

Canberra is a reminder that a country’s best-known city and its seat of government are not always the same place.
